\chapter{Knowing and Eating}
\label{ch:ar-knowing-and-eating}
\hlchaptermodality{30}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say the Arabic for 'he knew' and 'he ate', tell ʿarafa apart from ʿalima, and say plainly which of these verbs has an English cousin and which has none.}

Say akala with no new letters left to learn, run its doer and done-to forms, place it beside Hebrew akhal, and restate the ʿarafa root family and its Spanish loan.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ʿarafa]{\ar{عرف} (ʿarafa) — \textquotedblleft{}he knew,\textquotedblright{} and a root that crossed into Spain}

\label{lesson:AR-C30-arafa}



\begin{quote}
Back to a plain, regular root after three weak ones — and to a word that split into two where English has only one.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — The letters in this word}
One new letter, and it belongs to a family already half-known.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ar{ع}} (\emph{ʿayn}) — the throat-tightening sound with no English equal, met in \emph{ʿalaykum} and \emph{ʿafwan}.
  \item \textbf{\ar{ر}} (\emph{rāʾ}) — the tapped \emph{r}, a non-joiner.
  \item \textbf{\ar{ف}} (\emph{fāʾ}) — the new one: a small loop with a tail, carrying \textbf{one dot above}, sounding like English \emph{f}. Its partner is \textbf{\ar{ق}} (\emph{qāf}) from the \emph{qāla} lesson: mid-word the two bodies are the same shape, and only the dots separate them — \textbf{one} dot for \emph{f}, \textbf{two} for \emph{q}. A fourth dots-family.
\end{itemize}

Right to left: \emph{ʿayn}, \emph{rāʾ}, \emph{fāʾ} — \emph{ʿa-ra-fa}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{عَرَفَ}} (\emph{ʿarafa}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{he knew, he recognised}\textquotedblright{} — the plain \emph{faʿala} shape, no weak letters, root \textbf{\ar{ع}-\ar{ر}-\ar{ف}}. Its family:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ar{مَعْرِفة}} (\emph{maʿrifa}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{knowledge},\textquotedblright{} the \emph{ma-} shape.
  \item \textbf{\ar{عُرْف}} (\emph{ʿurf}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{custom},\textquotedblright{} what is commonly known.
  \item \textbf{\ar{العَرِيف}} (\emph{al-ʿarīf}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{the one who knows},\textquotedblright{} the expert or overseer. Spanish took the word in during the centuries of Arab rule and keeps it as \textbf{alarife}, \textquotedblleft{}master builder.\textquotedblright{} The palace gardens above Granada, the \textbf{Generalife}, are usually read as \textbf{\ar{جَنّة} \ar{العَرِيف}} (\emph{jannat al-ʿarīf}), \textquotedblleft{}the garden of the ʿarīf\textquotedblright{} — though scholars disagree about that second element, so treat it as the leading reading, not a settled one.
\end{itemize}

Arabic splits \textquotedblleft{}know\textquotedblright{} in two. \textbf{\ar{عَرَفَ}} is knowing a \emph{person} or a \emph{place} — recognising. Knowing a \emph{fact} is a different verb, \textbf{\ar{عَلِمَ}} (\emph{ʿalima}). Spanish cuts the same way with \emph{conocer} and \emph{saber}, French with \emph{connaître} and \emph{savoir}; English collapses both into one word. That second root gives \textbf{\ar{عالِم}} (\emph{ʿālim}), \textquotedblleft{}a scholar,\textquotedblright{} whose plural \textbf{\ar{عُلَماء}} (\emph{ʿulamāʾ}) English borrowed as \textbf{ulema}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the dots — \ar{ف} one dot, \ar{ق} two dots, one body between them
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ʿarafa\textquotedblright{} — he recognised — beside \textquotedblleft{}ʿalima,\textquotedblright{} he knew a fact
  \item the loan — al-ʿarīf, Spanish alarife, the Generalife in Granada
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What tells \textbf{\ar{ف}} and \textbf{\ar{ق}} apart? (\textbf{The dots} — one above for \emph{f}, two for \emph{q}.) Which of Arabic's two \textquotedblleft{}know\textquotedblright{} verbs is \emph{ʿarafa}, and what languages make the same split? (\textbf{Recognising a person or place}, against \emph{ʿalima} for a fact — as \textbf{Spanish} \emph{conocer/saber} and \textbf{French} \emph{connaître/savoir} do.) What Spanish word and what Granada palace carry \textbf{al-ʿarīf}? (\textbf{Alarife}, \textquotedblleft{}master builder,\textquotedblright{} and the \textbf{Generalife}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[akala]{\ar{أكل} (akala) — \textquotedblleft{}he ate,\textquotedblright{} and an honest word about cousins}

\label{lesson:AR-C30-akala}



\begin{quote}
The sixth and last verb of the set — and the one that needs no new letters at all, which is what a course built on words rather than alphabets eventually earns you.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — The letters in this word}
\textbf{Nothing new.} Every shape here has been taught already.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ar{أ}} — \emph{alif} with \textbf{hamza} riding on top, the glottal catch, opening the word with a clean \emph{a}.
  \item \textbf{\ar{ك}} (\emph{kāf}) — the angular \emph{k}.
  \item \textbf{\ar{ل}} (\emph{lām}) — the tall hook.
\end{itemize}

Right to left: \emph{a-ka-la}. Six chapters ago this word would have needed a lesson of its own just to be sounded out; now it reads itself.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{أَكَلَ}} (\emph{akala}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{he ate}.\textquotedblright{} Root \textbf{\ar{أ}-\ar{ك}-\ar{ل}}, and the plain \emph{faʿala} shape once more. Its family runs through the patterns already collected:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ar{أَكْل}} (\emph{akl}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{eating},\textquotedblright{} and so \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{food}.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textbf{\ar{مَأْكُولات}} (\emph{maʾkūlāt}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{foodstuffs},\textquotedblright{} the \textbf{done-to} shape from \emph{maqūl}, made plural: the things that get eaten.
  \item \textbf{\ar{آكِل}} (\emph{ākil}) — \textquotedblleft{}an \textbf{eater},\textquotedblright{} the \textbf{doer} shape, where the root's own \emph{alif} and the pattern's \emph{alif} fuse into the long \textbf{\ar{آ}}.
\end{itemize}

Now the honest part, because a false cousin is worse than none: \textbf{there is no English relative of this word.} Arabic and English are not related languages, and almost none of these six verbs has an English descendant — what English took from Arabic were nouns for goods and sciences, not everyday verbs. What \emph{akala} does have is a \textbf{Semitic} twin: Hebrew \textbf{\he{אָכַל}} (\emph{akhal}), \textquotedblleft{}he ate,\textquotedblright{} the same three consonants in the same order, with the Hebrew noun \emph{okhel}, \textquotedblleft{}food,\textquotedblright{} standing beside Arabic \emph{akl} — the same family resemblance heard in \emph{salām} and \emph{shalom}, and in \emph{yad} and \emph{yad}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}akala\textquotedblright{} — he ate — then \textquotedblleft{}akl,\textquotedblright{} food
  \item the two patterns — \textquotedblleft{}ākil,\textquotedblright{} an eater; \textquotedblleft{}maʾkūlāt,\textquotedblright{} foodstuffs
  \item the honest cousin — no English relative, but Hebrew \textquotedblleft{}akhal\textquotedblright{}
  \item all six — dhahaba, jāʾa, qāla, raʾā, ʿarafa, akala
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What two pattern-shapes give \textbf{\ar{آكِل}} and \textbf{\ar{مَأْكُولات}}, and what do they mean? (\textbf{Doer} and \textbf{done-to} — \textquotedblleft{}an eater\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}foodstuffs.\textquotedblright{}) Does \emph{akala} have an English cousin? (\textbf{No} — Arabic and English are unrelated; claiming one would be inventing it.) What is its Semitic twin? (\textbf{Hebrew \he{אָכַל}}, \emph{akhal}, \textquotedblleft{}he ate.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
